learning: If oval finish stays at or above 95% with fewer off-track exits, speed is still the cheapest lever and radius can go to 0.05 m. If s-bend or slalom off-track exits rise while max_error stays near 0.06 m, speed is outrunning steering, so the next step is radius 0.040 m with a wider track or a different spread, not more speed.
notes: Iteration 5 controller and layout, with wheel_radius raised from 0.040 to 0.045 m as the only change. The sensor layout, track, mass and controller are unchanged so the radius effect can be read directly against iteration 5.
rationale: The best-supported design is iteration 5 (score 422.9): five sensors at y=0.07 m, x = ±0.036 m, 16 mm footprint, track 0.10 m, mass 0.5 kg, radius 0.040 m. Iteration 4 showed radius 0.035 to 0.040 m lifted oval finish from 65% to 80%. Iteration 5 showed mass 0.6 to 0.5 kg lifted it to 95%. Iteration 6 (0.4 kg) cut s-bend progress from 0.72 to 0.59, and iteration 7 (track 0.09 m) cut oval finish to 60%, so both stay ruled out. Iteration 8 (spread ±0.045 m) cut slalom line losses from 1.85 to 1.0 but dropped oval finish to 65%, so spread was not free. This iteration makes one change against iteration 5: wheel_radius 0.040 to 0.045 m, as the Builder specified. The controller is kept at the iteration 5 values (kp 3.5, ki 0.05, kd 0.5, base_speed 1.6, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction). The larger radius raises ground speed per wheel rotation by about 12%. The steering gains are not rescaled, since the wheel radius does not change the turn equation. Expected, not measured: oval finish holds at or above 95% and completion time drops. The risk is more off-track exits on the s-bend and slalom if speed outruns steering. I have not measured this design.
